claims.source: Clinical trials in myocardial infarction patients show a correlation of inflammatory markers with extent of the myocardial damage (Sánchez et al., 2006) and with short- and long-term mortality (Mueller et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Mueller et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Depletion of macrophages by anti-CSF1R treatment is associated with worsened cardiac function in a model of pressure overload induced heart failure.
claims.source: In line with our findings, depletion of macrophages by anti-CSF1R treatment was associated with worsened cardiac function in a model of pressure overload induced heart failure (Revelo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Revelo et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Depletion of recruited macrophages only in the initial phase of myocardial infarction improved cardiac healing in Ccr2DTR mice.
claims.source: Controversially, a recent study in which monocytes were depleted using DT-injections in Ccr2DTR mice reported beneficial effects on cardiac outcome after MI in mice (Bajpai et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Bajpai et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury.
claims.source: In line with this, Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury, which was associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema (Dimitrijevic et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Dimitrijevic et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Reduced neutrophil recruitment in Ccr2-deficient mice after brain I/R injury is associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema.
claims.source: In line with this, Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury, which was associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema (Dimitrijevic et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Dimitrijevic et al., 2007.

results.result: The majority (~80%) of cardiac macrophages in healthy adult mice are derived from yolk sac erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs), with ~20% derived from definitive hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), establishing that most resident cardiac macrophages are of early embryonic origin.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by complementary lineage tracing experiments using two independent reporter systems (Tnfsf11aCre and Flt3Cre), with quantitative flow cytometry data showing ~80% YFP+ macrophages in EMP tracing and ~20% in HSC tracing. The conclusion logically follows from the combined data.

results.result: The Csf1rΔFIRE mouse model specifically depletes ~90% of cardiac macrophages without affecting monocyte or neutrophil numbers, and the depleted macrophages are specifically EMP-derived resident macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are supported by flow cytometry and histology data showing selective macrophage depletion in ΔFIRE mice. The specificity is confirmed by crossing with lineage tracing mice showing that depleted cells are YFP+ EMP-derived macrophages, while monocytes and neutrophils remain unaffected.

results.result: Acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages using diphtheria toxin in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-DTR mice results in premature death within 24 hours and induces a systemic inflammatory response syndrome-like phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8 are supported by survival data showing 100% mortality within 24 hours (n=6) and physiological measurements showing body temperature and cardiac volume changes. This establishes that DT-mediated depletion is not viable for studying resident macrophage function.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing reveals that ΔFIRE mice specifically lack two macrophage clusters expressing homeostatic and antigen-presenting genes, which correspond to ~90% of YFP+ EMP-derived macrophages, while other macrophage populations and monocytes remain unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are supported by comprehensive scRNA-seq analysis showing specific cluster depletion in ΔFIRE mice that correlates with YFP expression patterns in lineage tracing. The specificity is confirmed by unchanged gene expression and cell numbers in monocytes and inflammatory macrophage clusters.

results.result: Absence of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice is associated with altered gene expression in non-macrophage immune cells (T-cells, B-cells, NK cells) and reduced overall phagocytic capacity in the heart.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 are supported by scRNA-seq data showing differential gene expression in non-macrophage clusters and computed phagocytosis scores. However, the functional significance of these changes in baseline conditions requires further investigation.

results.result: Absence of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice negatively influences cardiac remodeling after I/R injury, with LVEF and stroke volume improving in controls but remaining unchanged or worsening in ΔFIRE mice from day 6 to day 30 post-injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C21 are supported by longitudinal PET imaging data showing differential cardiac function trajectories between control and ΔFIRE mice. The data demonstrate impaired functional recovery in ΔFIRE mice, indicating a detrimental role of resident macrophage absence on cardiac remodeling.

results.result: Infarct size, measured by both viability defect (PET) and fibrotic area (histology), is not different between control and ΔFIRE mice 30 days after I/R injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C23 are supported by both PET imaging and histological quantification showing no significant difference in infarct size. This finding is important as it distinguishes the effect of resident macrophages on remodeling from their effect on infarct size.

results.result: After I/R injury, resident macrophages remain depleted in the remote zone of ΔFIRE mice, but bone marrow-derived macrophages are recruited normally to the infarct and border zones, where they represent the main population (~75% in infarct zone at day 30).
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 are supported by immunohistology and lineage tracing data showing sustained resident macrophage depletion in remote zones but normal recruitment of BM-derived macrophages to injury sites. The spatial gradient of BM-derived macrophages (75% infarct, 50% border, 35% remote) is well-documented.

results.result: Resident (CD45.2+) and recruited (CD45.1+) macrophages exhibit profound transcriptional differences after I/R injury, with resident macrophages expressing homeostatic genes and upregulating development/homeostasis-related pathways, while recruited macrophages show inflammatory and immune defense-related gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 are supported by bulk RNA-sequencing of sorted macrophage populations from bone marrow chimeric mice. The differential gene expression and GO enrichment analyses clearly demonstrate distinct functional programs in the two populations.

results.result: Two days after I/R injury, ΔFIRE mice show reduced homeostatic macrophages but unaltered inflammatory macrophages, with altered gene expression across immune cell types including reduced anti-inflammatory genes (Chil3, Lcn2), increased pro-apoptotic genes (Bcl2a1a, Bcl2a1d), and increased inflammasome activation in neutrophils.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by scRNA-seq analysis showing cluster-specific changes and computed inflammasome scores. The data demonstrate that resident macrophage absence alters the inflammatory landscape beyond just macrophage populations.

results.result: Absence of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice markedly reduces ligand-receptor interactions and communication signal strength from homeostatic and antigen-presenting macrophage clusters to neutrophils and lymphocytes, while BM-derived inflammatory macrophage communication and transcriptional profiles remain largely unaltered.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis from scRNA-seq data showing reduced intercellular communication from resident macrophage clusters but not from recruited macrophage clusters. This provides mechanistic insight into how resident macrophages influence other immune cells.

results.result: Continuous CSF1R inhibition with PLX5622 depletes cardiac macrophages within 7 days in healthy hearts and maintains depletion of both resident and recruited macrophages in all cardiac zones (remote, border, infarct) after I/R injury, without affecting neutrophil recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by flow cytometry and immunohistology data showing effective macrophage depletion at baseline and after injury in all cardiac zones. The specificity for macrophages is confirmed by unaltered neutrophil numbers.

results.result: Combined absence of resident and recruited macrophages (PLX5622 treatment) results in increased infarct size and severe deterioration of cardiac function, with LVEF reduced at day 6 and remaining strongly impaired at day 30 after I/R injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by PET imaging and histology data showing worse outcomes with combined macrophage depletion compared to resident-only depletion. This demonstrates the beneficial role of recruited macrophages in limiting infarct size.

results.result: Comparison of ΔFIRE mice (resident macrophage depletion only) versus PLX5622-treated mice (both resident and recruited macrophage depletion) reveals that sole absence of resident macrophages has limited impact on cardiac remodeling, while combined absence significantly increases infarct size and worsens cardiac function, highlighting the beneficial effect of recruited macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by comparative analysis of the two depletion models showing differential effects on infarct size and cardiac function. The inference that recruited macrophages are beneficial is logically sound based on the worse outcomes when both populations are depleted.

results.result: The study concludes that resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses to improve cardiac remodeling, while recruited macrophages determine infarct size after I/R injury, representing distinct beneficial functions of the two macrophage populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 represent the main conclusions synthesized from multiple lines of evidence: ΔFIRE mice show impaired remodeling but unchanged infarct size, while PLX5622 treatment shows both impaired remodeling and increased infarct size. The conclusions are well-supported by the collective data.

results.result: The manuscript provides extensive background context through citations to prior work on macrophage biology, cardiovascular disease, myocardial infarction pathophysiology, macrophage ontogeny, and previous depletion studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C82 are all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific context and rationale for the current study. The accuracy of these citations would need to be verified against the original sources, but they appear appropriate for establishing background knowledge.

results.result: The authors used lineage tracing models (Tnfsf11aCre and Flt3Cre) to demonstrate that approximately 80% of cardiac macrophages are derived from yolk sac EMPs and 20% from definitive HSCs, concluding that the majority of resident cardiac macrophages are of early embryonic origin.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly affirm the use of 'state-of-the-art fate-mapping models' and recognize the lineage tracing data as solid evidence. Reviewer 1 states the evidence is 'solid with the use of the FIRE mouse model in combination with fate-mapping,' and Reviewer 2 highlights the 'major strength' of the fate-mapping approach. No concerns are raised about these foundational lineage tracing claims.

results.result: The authors validated the ΔFIRE mouse model by confirming ~90% reduction in cardiac macrophages (specifically EMP-derived) while monocytes and neutrophils remain unaltered, establishing this as a model to selectively study resident macrophages.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise the ΔFIRE model as a 'major strength' (Reviewer 2) that 'for the first time, allows specific targeting of only fetal-derived macrophages.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'showed a reduction of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice' and acknowledges the 'robust methodology.' The specificity of the depletion to EMP-derived macrophages is accepted without critique.

results.result: Acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages using diphtheria toxin in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-DTR mice resulted in premature death within 24 hours and a systemic inflammatory response syndrome-like phenotype, demonstrating that acute depletion is not viable.
results.evaluation: While not explicitly discussed by reviewers, this finding is presented as justification for using the ΔFIRE model instead of DT-mediated depletion. Reviewers accept the ΔFIRE model without questioning why DT depletion was not used, implicitly supporting the rationale that acute DT depletion is problematic. No reviewer challenges these claims.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing revealed that two clusters of macrophages expressing homeostatic and antigen-presenting genes are specifically ablated in ΔFIRE mice, representing ~90% of YFP+ cells from the EMP lineage tracing model, while other macrophage clusters (Cx3cr1hi, Ccr2lowLy6clo, Ccr2hiLy6chi) and monocytes remain unaffected.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes the authors 'characterized its macrophages populations via scRNAseq at baseline conditions' and acknowledges the 'robust methodology encompassing state of the art immunological methods.' Reviewer 2 states 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' implicitly accepting the scRNA-seq characterization of which populations are depleted.

results.result: Absence of resident macrophages in ΔFIRE mice is associated with changes in gene expression in non-macrophage immune cells (T-cells, B-cells, NK cells) and reduced overall phagocytic capacity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk in response to injury,' directly supporting these claims about altered immune cell gene expression. No reviewer questions the phagocytosis score or changes in non-macrophage populations.

results.result: After I/R injury, cardiac function (LVEF and stroke volume) improved in control mice but remained unchanged or worsened in ΔFIRE mice from day 6 to day 30, indicating that absence of resident macrophages negatively influenced cardiac remodeling. However, infarct size (measured by PET viability defect and histological fibrosis) was not different between groups at 30 days.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'differential effects on echocardiographic function 6 and 30 days after I/R injury' and Reviewer 2 states 'the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' directly confirming both the functional impairment and the lack of difference in infarct size. All reviewers accept these findings without challenge.

results.result: After I/R injury, macrophages remain largely absent in the remote zone of ΔFIRE mice, but bone marrow-derived macrophages are recruited to the infarct area (representing ~75% of macrophages in the infarct zone, ~50% in border zone, and ~35% in remote zone at 30 days), with recruitment unaltered in ΔFIRE mice compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'Via flow cytometry and histology the authors confirmed existing evidence of increased bone marrow-derived macrophage infiltration to the heart, specifically to the ischemic myocardium. Macrophage population in ΔFIRE mice after I/R injury were only changed in the remote zone.' This directly supports the spatial distribution and recruitment findings. No concerns are raised about the lineage tracing data showing BM-derived macrophage proportions.

results.result: Bulk RNA-sequencing of CD45.1+ (recruited) and CD45.2+ (resident) macrophages 2 days after I/R injury revealed profound transcriptional differences: resident macrophages upregulate homeostasis-related genes (Timd4, Lyve1, Cd163, Retnla) and development/homeostasis GO terms, while recruited macrophages upregulate inflammatory/host defense GO terms and processes related to innate and adaptive immunity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'Further RNAseq data on resident or recruited macrophages showed transcriptional differences between both cell types in terms of homeostasis-related genes and inflammation.' This directly supports the bulk RNA-seq findings. Reviewer 2 states the findings are 'in line with the current idea in the field that macrophages of different origins have distinct functions in tissues,' affirming the biological interpretation.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-sequencing 2 days after I/R injury showed that homeostatic macrophages are reduced in ΔFIRE mice while Ccr2hiLy6chi inflammatory macrophages are unaltered. In ΔFIRE mice, anti-inflammatory genes (Chil3, Lcn2) are reduced and pro-apoptotic/inflammatory genes (Bcl2a1a, Bcl2a1d) are increased across immune cell clusters. Neutrophils show increased inflammasome activation, and ligand-receptor interactions from resident macrophage clusters to neutrophils/lymphocytes are markedly reduced, while BM-derived macrophage communication and transcriptional profiles remain unaltered.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states '2 days after I/R protocol ΔFIRE mice showed an enhanced pro inflammatory phenotype in the RNAseq data,' directly supporting the findings of altered inflammatory gene expression and neutrophil inflammasome activation. Reviewer 2 states 'the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk in response to injury,' confirming the ligand-receptor interaction findings. No concerns are raised about the scRNA-seq analysis after injury.

results.result: Pharmacological depletion of all macrophages (both resident and recruited) using CSF1R inhibitor PLX5622 resulted in absence of cardiac macrophages within 7 days in healthy hearts and sustained depletion in all cardiac zones after I/R injury (without altering neutrophil recruitment). This was associated with increased infarct size, deteriorated cardiac function (reduced LVEF at both day 6 and day 30), demonstrating worse outcomes than ΔFIRE mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'Depleting all macrophage using a Csf1r inhibitor resulted in a reduced cardiac function and increased fibrosis,' directly supporting these findings. The comparison between ΔFIRE (resident only) and PLX5622 (resident + recruited) depletion is central to the manuscript's conclusions and is accepted by all reviewers without challenge.

results.result: By comparing ΔFIRE mice (resident macrophage depletion only) with PLX5622-treated mice (both resident and recruited macrophage depletion), the authors conclude that sole absence of resident macrophages has limited negative impact on cardiac remodeling, while absence of both populations results in significantly increased infarct size and deteriorated function. This demonstrates that recruited macrophages have a beneficial effect and determine infarct size, while resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses to improve cardiac remodeling.
results.evaluation: This is the central conclusion of the manuscript and is explicitly supported by all reviewers. Reviewer 1 states the study 'provides important findings on the distinct functions exerted by resident and recruited macrophages during cardiac healing.' Reviewer 2 notes 'the data show that the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size but instead is altering the immune cell crosstalk,' and states the findings are 'in line with the current idea in the field that macrophages of different origins have distinct functions.' Reviewer 3 calls the work 'important for the field of cardiac injury.'

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C1-C3 regarding lineage tracing experiments. Both evaluations recognize the solid evidence from fate-mapping models (Tnfsf11aCre and Flt3Cre) and affirm the complementary approach as a major strength of the study.

Perfect agreement on claims C4-C6 regarding ΔFIRE model specificity. Both evaluations praise the selective depletion of EMP-derived macrophages as a major strength and accept the specificity demonstrated by flow cytometry and lineage tracing data.

Agreement on claims C7-C8 regarding DT-mediated depletion lethality. OpenEval explicitly supports the survival and physiological data, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this rationale by endorsing the ΔFIRE model without questioning the absence of DT depletion experiments.

Perfect agreement on claims C9-C15 regarding baseline scRNA-seq characterization. Both evaluations recognize the robust methodology and accept the specific cluster depletion patterns and correlation with YFP expression in ΔFIRE mice.

Perfect agreement on claims C16-C17 regarding altered immune cell gene expression at baseline. Both evaluations support the findings of changes in non-macrophage populations and altered immune cell crosstalk, though OpenEval notes the functional significance requires further investigation.

Strong agreement on claims C18-C21 regarding impaired cardiac functional recovery. Both evaluations accept the PET imaging data showing differential trajectories between control and ΔFIRE mice. Peer review R6 also addresses C22-C23 (infarct size), which OpenEval covers separately in R7.

Agreement on claims C22-C23 regarding unchanged infarct size in ΔFIRE mice. OpenEval emphasizes this distinguishes remodeling effects from infarct size effects. Peer reviewers explicitly confirm 'the absence of resident macrophages is not influencing infarct size,' grouping this with functional outcomes.

Perfect agreement on claims C24-C31 regarding spatial distribution of macrophage populations after injury. Both evaluations accept the lineage tracing and immunohistology data showing sustained resident macrophage depletion in remote zones and normal BM-derived macrophage recruitment to injury sites.

Perfect agreement on claims C32-C37 regarding transcriptional differences between resident and recruited macrophages. Both evaluations support the bulk RNA-seq findings showing distinct functional programs, with peer reviewers noting this aligns with current understanding in the field.

Strong agreement on claims C38-C43 regarding enhanced pro-inflammatory phenotype after injury. Both evaluations support the scRNA-seq findings of cluster-specific changes and inflammasome activation. Peer review R9 also addresses C44-C47 (ligand-receptor interactions), which OpenEval covers separately in R11.

Agreement on claims C44-C47 regarding reduced intercellular communication from resident macrophage clusters. OpenEval provides detailed support for ligand-receptor interaction analysis. Peer reviewers confirm altered immune cell crosstalk findings, grouping these with inflammatory phenotype changes.

Strong agreement on claims C48-C51 regarding effective macrophage depletion with PLX5622 treatment. Both evaluations accept the flow cytometry and histology data. Peer review R10 groups these with C52-C55 (functional outcomes), which OpenEval covers separately in R13.

Agreement on claims C52-C55 regarding worse outcomes with combined macrophage depletion (PLX5622). Both evaluations support the findings of reduced cardiac function and increased fibrosis when both resident and recruited macrophages are depleted.

Strong agreement on claims C56-C59 regarding differential effects of the two depletion models. Both evaluations accept the comparative analysis showing recruited macrophages are beneficial. Peer review R11 also addresses C60-C61 (main conclusions), which OpenEval covers separately in R15.

Perfect agreement on claims C60-C61 representing the main conclusions. Both evaluations strongly support the central finding that resident and recruited macrophages have distinct functions. All peer reviewers explicitly endorse these conclusions as important contributions to the field.

OpenEval evaluated claims C62-C82 regarding background literature citations and found them appropriately supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these background claims, as peer reviewers focused on experimental findings rather than citation accuracy.
